title: 03 — Iceberg Catalogs and Interoperability
html:
03 — Iceberg Catalogs and Interoperability

The one idea: the table format made files open. The catalog decides who can commit, who can read, and with what credentials. In 2026 the catalog is where interoperability is won or lost, and the Iceberg REST protocol is the common language.

1. What it is

A catalog maps a table name to its current metadata pointer and performs the atomic swap on commit (see 01). Modern catalogs do much more:

  • Govern access: who may read and write which tables.
  • Vend credentials: give each engine short-lived storage access for one table.
  • Plan scans on the server.
  • Coordinate commits that span several tables.

The Iceberg REST catalog protocol is an OpenAPI specification that any engine can call, so the engine no longer needs a catalog-specific plugin.

2. Why it matters

  • One table, many engines: Databricks writes, Snowflake or DuckDB reads. It works only if every engine talks to the same catalog.
  • Security: with credential vending, engines never hold long-lived storage keys.
  • Lock-in moves up a level: files are open, but a catalog that only one vendor's engines can use still locks you in.

3. The main ideas

3.1 What the REST protocol covers

---
title: Iceberg REST catalog — what an engine asks for
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Engine (Spark, DuckDB, Snowflake)
    participant C as REST catalog
    participant S as Object storage
    E->>C: GET /v1/config
    C-->>E: Defaults and overrides
    E->>C: Load table fin.nav
    C-->>E: metadata location and short-lived storage credentials
    E->>S: Read manifests and data files with vended credentials
    E->>C: Commit (requirements + updates)
    C-->>E: 200 OK, or 409 conflict, then retry
  • Server-owned commits: the client sends requirements (for example, "current snapshot must still be X") and updates. The server checks them atomically. Per the Iceberg docs, this is what makes server-side conflict resolution, multi-table commits and credential vending (or remote signing) possible.
  • Credential vending: the catalog returns storage credentials scoped to one table for a short time, so a leaked token exposes little.
  • Server-side scan planning: the catalog plans the scan and returns the file list. A 2026 overview reports that a REST scan-planning client arrived in Iceberg 1.11.
  • Support varies: "supports REST" means different endpoints in different products. Apache Gravitino's REST server docs, for example, listed multi-table transactions as not yet implemented in version 1.2.1. Check the endpoint list for each catalog.

3.2 The catalogs you will meet

Catalog What it is (checked 2026-10-26)
Unity Catalog (Databricks) Governs managed and foreign Iceberg tables and Delta tables. Exposes an Iceberg REST endpoint for outside engines (Spark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake, DuckDB). Databricks lists managed Iceberg tables as GA
Apache Polaris Open-source Iceberg REST catalog. Graduated to a top-level Apache project on 19 February 2026
Lakekeeper Apache-licensed REST catalog in Rust (built on iceberg-rust), with OpenFGA or OPA for permissions
Apache Gravitino Metadata lake with an Iceberg REST service
Project Nessie Catalog with Git-like branches across tables
AWS Glue, S3 Tables AWS-managed catalogs and Iceberg storage
SQL or JDBC catalog A plain database table of pointers. Good for laptops and tests (PyIceberg SqlCatalog)

3.3 Iceberg and Delta: converging

  • UniForm: Delta tables that also write Iceberg metadata, so Iceberg clients can read them. Delta 4.2 (April 2026) moved UniForm's Iceberg metadata generation to commit time (synchronous), and deprecated Hive Metastore support for UniForm.
  • Catalog-managed tables (Delta 4.1 onward): the catalog becomes the coordinator and source of truth for table state, the model Iceberg pioneered. Delta 4.3 routes those operations through Unity Catalog's Delta REST APIs.
  • Foreign tables: Unity Catalog can govern Iceberg tables whose metadata another catalog owns (Glue, Snowflake, Hive), and share them.

3.4 Choosing for a platform that must stay open

  1. One owning catalog per table. Others read through REST or federation.
  2. Write with the engine that owns the table. Read from anywhere.
  3. Prefer credential vending over shared storage keys.
  4. Test the exact path (engine, catalog, table version) before you promise a client that "any engine can read it".

4. Working code

There is no runnable code here, because a REST catalog needs a server. The PyIceberg configuration below shows the shape of a REST client. It is not run. The endpoint and credential are placeholders. For Unity Catalog, use the path given in the Databricks "access tables from Iceberg clients" documentation for your workspace.

# Not run: needs a reachable REST catalog. Never hard-code tokens: read them from a vault or environment.
import os
from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

catalog = load_catalog("uc", **{
    "type": "rest",
    "uri": os.environ["ICEBERG_REST_URI"],           # the catalog's REST endpoint
    "token": os.environ["ICEBERG_REST_TOKEN"],        # short-lived token from your identity provider
    "warehouse": os.environ["ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE"],     # the catalog name, in Unity Catalog's case
})
table = catalog.load_table("gold.fund_nav_daily")
print(table.metadata.format_version, table.current_snapshot())

5. Common mistakes

  1. Two catalogs writing to one table. Their pointers diverge, and one silently loses commits.
  2. Static storage keys in engine configuration. Use vended credentials, or at least scoped, short-lived ones.
  3. Assuming every REST catalog supports every endpoint. Check multi-table commits, scan planning and views separately.
  4. Assuming every reader handles v3 because the catalog does. The engine has to support the table version too.
  5. Treating UniForm as a two-way bridge. Iceberg clients read UniForm tables. Writes go through Delta.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

Draw your target setup: which catalog owns each layer's tables (Bronze, Silver, Gold), which engines write, which read, and through which protocol. For each pair, note one thing you would test before relying on it (format version, credential vending, deletion-vector support).

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does the REST protocol let a catalog do that a plain pointer store cannot?
  2. What is credential vending, and why is it safer?
  3. When did Apache Polaris become a top-level Apache project?
  4. What changed for UniForm in Delta 4.2?
  5. Why should exactly one catalog own each table?

Answers

  1. Resolve conflicts on the server, commit across several tables at once, vend credentials or sign requests, and plan scans.
  2. The catalog hands each engine short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table, so nothing long-lived or broad can leak.
  3. On 19 February 2026, per the Apache announcement.
  4. Iceberg metadata is generated synchronously at commit time, and Hive Metastore support for UniForm was deprecated.
  5. The catalog holds the only commit pointer. Two owners means two diverging histories.
